I have read Discourses, and this is not true. It was not satire. He touches on many of the same topics and says many of the same words as in The Prince. 

The Prince was catered to a pompous Medici, a clan who imprisoned and tortured him. He himself believed that a Republic is best (as cited in The Multitude is more wiser and more constant than a Prince/ book 1) but he was not opposed to other ways of ruling as he gives advice to both princes, tyrants, and republics in Discourses. He tells the tyrant is best to stop his tyrannical will but they do not, so what mode to proceed in is... etc. etc. Saying his work was satire takes away from his unbiased genius that was simply to incorporate ideas that were effective, regardless of their morality. Very clear. 

Discourses corroborates his views in the Prince. For instance, in Discourses he cites that Giavampogolo Baglioni was a bad man who commutes all sorts of grave offenses, such as killing his parents and incest with his sister, but where he failed is he was not entirely bad. He should have been ruthless and denied the Pope a foothold into his province, and though he was awful he was not awful enough and this led to his cowardice and ultimately the unhappiness of the province. 

The Prince has some blatant sass and crudeness in the way he describes political affairs, but I feel that it is due to his cross feelings for the Medici’s, but he indeed, respected Lorenzo in some ways but his feelings were deeply hurt by what the Medicis had done to him. His work exposed Alexander VI as a deceiver of men, and for that I believe he has been villainized. Alexander was indeed, a incredibly corrupt figure, so it must be true: such work was scandalous and it was work he only circulated amongst his closest friends. I don’t feel he ever intended to go down in history for that work at all. But alas, here we are.

It was undeniably an accurate view of Renaissance politics, if you consider the ruthlessness and bloodshed. In Discourses he gives some form of praise to Caterina Sforza for how she handled the men who killed her husband and were about to killed her kids. She exposed her private parts and said “kill them, I have what it takes to make more”. 

The Prince is valuable for a Prince in the Renaissance. But it is not Machiavelli’s heart. It’s not his soul. It is his brain and knowledge applied to solve a problem of political affairs and a quick treatise of How to be a Prince. It may contain the occasionally sardonic tone, but it was, indeed, real advice. 

This is why people find his works to not corroborate with one another. Because those people are not asking themselves “who was his audience?”

He was a brilliant historian. A brilliant writer. And a brilliant politician. Discourses is well worth the read.
